text: This is a walkthrough of Study 1: validating code-optimization edits with a reduced build and reduced tests and benchmarks, chosen by deterministic rules, with no AI in the method.

There are five parts: what the literature and existing optimizers do; the future work the papers themselves name; the gap we found; the experiment designed on that gap, and its pilot results; and what comes next.
Part one. When code is optimized through many small edits, can each edit be checked with a reduced build and a reduced test and benchmark set, and still be trusted?

The study has three research questions. RQ1 is cost: what share of per-edit validation time goes to build, tests and benchmarks. RQ2 asks what existing techniques, used unchanged, save and miss. And RQ3 asks whether a new deterministic policy misses less than the best existing combination, at matched cost.

This is the one-page literature summary. It is a targeted review of primary sources, not a systematic one. It covers 138 references and 72 open-access papers, and includes searches of the ACM and IEEE digital libraries. Its main lesson: every reduction technique is safe only under stated assumptions. Incremental builds need complete dependencies. Regression test selection needs controlled conditions and fresh dependency data. And benchmark selection needs performance effects to stay where the coverage is.

This figure places the closest works on a grid. The top row holds decisions made per revision, using only the current change. The bottom row holds decisions that use state accumulated across edits. Study 1 sits in the highlighted band: a reduced check on every edit, and a full check when the accumulated change crosses a threshold.

Five works are closest. PerfAgent runs testmon-selected tests on every optimization iteration. But it never runs the full suite, and it reports no misses. NameRTS is the strongest Python selector found, cutting time by 45.6 percent. Sayedsalehi and colleagues, at Mozilla, flush a batch of performance tests when a learned risk sum passes a threshold. Our full-check trigger is a model-free variant of that. Fallahzadeh, Rigby and Adams find that selection misses up to 55 percent of failures. Ekstazi and testmon are the baselines.

The practice survey asked how existing optimizers build and verify each candidate edit. They pay one build per edit, except Codeflash and OpenEvolve, which have no build step. Only PerfAgent cuts tests per edit. None re-checks accepted edits together in its code, and no system reports build seconds.

Part two. What future work do the papers themselves state? PerfAgent names extending selective testing to native-extension coverage. Fallahzadeh and colleagues leave combining test optimization techniques, such as selection and batching, to future work. The Ekstazi authors leave a formal proof of its safety to future work. Kotinos lists the preconditions its dependency inference relies on. And a recent survey of agentic issue resolution says program-analysis test selection has not been integrated. The card gives the source of each line.

Part three: the gap. The gap is evidence of where existing reduction may become unsafe, when the edits are performance optimizations that build on each other. There are four suspected mechanisms. C5, the C-extension boundary: edits to C or Cython are invisible to testmon-style selection. C7, stale dependency data: reduced runs refresh only the tests that ran. This one is partial: Chittimalli and Harrold showed outdated coverage harms selection for a single version step. Our angle is how misses grow as the refresh interval lengthens over a chain of edits. C11, dropped benchmarks: covering the change is not enough. And C8, incremental rebuilds: setuptools and Cython rebuild by file timestamps, and ignore flag and directive changes.

What we do not claim: Not a better test selector. Not per-edit selection in optimization loops. Not periodic full runs. And not batching, or risk-based batch sizes. Claim C1 is narrowed. We concede that our full-check trigger is a model-free variant of the learned cumulative-risk batching of Sayedsalehi and colleagues. What we did not find is an evaluation of such a trigger on top of a per-edit reduced check, for chains of dependent edits, against fixed-k batching at matched cost.

One caveat on the search. It is targeted, not systematic. The ACM and IEEE libraries were searched, with 123 records screened, but Scopus and Web of Science were not. So any novelty means only this: not found in our recorded searches.

Part four: the experiment. It replays real historical optimization commits. Networkx is the pure-Python pilot. Bottleneck is the C-extension project. Its extension modules are generated from templates, so incremental builds are not trivial.

Tests and benchmarks are frozen at the base, and each step applies one commit's source change. The stated limit: this is a replay of independent historical commits, not a recorded optimization session.

Full validation is the oracle. The arms are: a full rebuild with all tests and benchmarks; an incremental build; testmon, as PerfAgent uses it; a naive changed-module rule; and static benchmark selection. These existing arms also run with a full check every k steps. Last is our policy, with an ablation for each of its three parts.

Now the pilot results, all preliminary. First, where the cost is. On networkx, benchmarks dominate. One full benchmark pass took 659 to 2,444 seconds over six measured passes, a median of about 730, against about 87 seconds for build plus serial tests: about 8 to 28 times. Most of it is setup. 87 to 96 percent of a pass is one module's 49 cases, and 80 to 94 percent of a pass is outside the timing loops. With setup cached, a pass would be about 1.5 to 2 times build plus tests; that is an estimate, not a measurement. The build is a minor lever: about 0.15 percent here, and 16 to 18 percent of build plus tests on bottleneck, before benchmarks. And the cost is itself noisy, for reasons not yet known.

Second, the oracle gap, starting with coverage. Of the 15 true optimizations among the 18 replayed edits, 9 change no function that any benchmark executes in the measured profile: 60 percent, with a confidence interval of 36 to 80 percent. So many, not most. By static call graph it is 4 of 15. So even full benchmarking cannot confirm many of these speed-ups with the project's own suite. This is established on networkx only; elsewhere it was not validly tested.

The second part of the gap is power. Of 10 frozen slowdowns, full benchmarking detects at most 3, 2 on target, and none in the pre-set bands. So the pre-registered result is that regression safety of reduced selection is not measurable on networkx with this set. Five of the seven misses are reached by no benchmark. The A/A run gave 0 false verdicts in 46, but only about 2 times slowdowns are reliably caught on the sampled heavy cases. A profile-completeness check flagged 1 comparison in 50. A post-hoc re-check did not confirm it, and the flag stands.

Third, functional test selection is a solved, modest win. Testmon is about 3.5 to 4 times cheaper than full validation end to end, not the 15 times that test-seconds suggest, and about 6 times on the worked edit. It misses 0 of 20 frozen mutants, with a 95 percent upper bound of 16.1 percent. Those mutants are caught almost by construction, so this is not a safety guarantee. The changed-module rule misses 2 of 20, through test-file naming. And PerfAgent already uses testmon per edit.

Fourth, the honest negatives for our policy. The fault model cannot tell selection rules apart, because every per-edit arm catches the mutants at injection by construction. And our policy, as implemented, costs more: 655 seconds against 330 for plain testmon. Counting benchmarks, batching is 1.7 to 6 times cheaper than per-edit arms, and our policy costs about twice batching, which depends on its profile selection collapsing to all benchmarks. It behaves like a full check every 4 edits, and accumulation showed no effect. There is no claim that it beats batching.

So the next step follows the evidence. First, a pre-registered replication of the coverage finding, because it was not validly tested outside networkx: measured profiles at each edit's parent, a stricter mining rule fixed before mining, and a check of each diff, before any decision to pivot. Then checkpoint re-profiling, a fault model that can separate selection rules, a measured setup-cached benchmark pass, and the remaining literature search, including the novelty risk. Later comes the AI-based study, measured against this deterministic baseline.
That is where Study 1 stands today.
